title: The Yoke of Babylon
summary: When envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon gather in Jerusalem, apparently to plan a revolt, Jeremiah appears wearing an ox yoke and tells them that the LORD, maker of the earth, has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar. Nations that bow under Babylon's yoke will live in their land; those that resist will be destroyed. He tells Zedekiah and the priests the same, and warns that the temple furnishings still in Jerusalem will be carried off too, though God will one day bring them back.
story: Chapters 27 to 29 form a unit about false prophecy in Zedekiah's early years, all tied to one question: how long will Babylon's rule last? Chapter 27 sets out Jeremiah's answer in a dramatic sign. Chapter 28 shows a rival prophet breaking the yoke in public. Chapter 29 carries the same message by letter to the exiles in Babylon. After the first deportation of 597 BC (chapter 24), the pressure in Jerusalem was to throw off Babylon quickly. Jeremiah's message is that God himself has placed the nations under Babylon for a set time (25:11-12), and that resisting it is resisting him.
historical:
Verse 1 in the BSB dates this word to the beginning of Zedekiah's reign. Most Hebrew manuscripts actually read Jehoiakim there, while the Greek translation lacks the verse altogether; translations like the BSB follow a few manuscripts and the context, since verses 3 and 12 name Zedekiah and 28:1 places the related events in his fourth year, about 594 or 593 BC. In those years Nebuchadnezzar faced unrest; the Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform record of his reign, reports a revolt within Babylon around 595 or 594 BC, and a new pharaoh, Psammetichus II, took the Egyptian throne in 595 BC. Small states in the region may have seen a chance to break free, and the envoys in verse 3 were in Jerusalem to discuss it. The plan came to nothing for the moment, but Zedekiah did rebel a few years later, which led to the siege and fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC.

The temple furnishings named in verse 19 (the two bronze pillars, the great bronze basin called the sea, and the wheeled stands) were made in Solomon's day (1 Kings 7:15-39). Some of the temple's gold vessels were taken in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:13); the rest, including the bronze, went in 586 BC (Jeremiah 52:17-23). Ezra 1:7-11 records Cyrus returning thousands of vessels to Jerusalem. Verse 7's son and grandson describe a limited dynasty: Nebuchadnezzar's son Amel-Marduk (the Evil-merodach of 52:31) reigned briefly, a few short reigns followed, and Babylon fell to Persia in 539 BC. Many readers take the phrase as an idiom for a few generations.
cultural:
A yoke was a wooden bar laid across the necks of a pair of oxen and tied on with leather straps or ropes, so the animals could be harnessed to pull a plow or cart. It was a common picture of subjection to a master or empire. Jeremiah's yoke was a prophetic sign-act, a message acted out in public, like his linen belt in chapter 13 and the smashed jar in chapter 19. The envoys would have understood it at once.

Verse 9 lists the experts that neighboring nations consulted before war: prophets, diviners, interpreters of dreams, mediums, and sorcerers. Diviners read omens in the livers of sacrificed animals, the flight of birds, or the stars; mediums claimed to consult the dead. Israel's law forbade all of these (Deuteronomy 18:9-14). Jeremiah sets Judah's own prophets alongside them, a humbling comparison: when they promise what the LORD has not said, they are no better than foreign soothsayers.
literary: The chapter has three addresses with the same message, each ending in a warning about false prophets. The first goes to the foreign kings (verses 2 to 11), the second to Zedekiah (12 to 15), and the third to the priests and people (16 to 22). The key words repeat: “serve” appears again and again, as does the call to put the neck under the yoke, and three times the prophets are said to prophesy “a lie.” Jeremiah's argument moves from creation to history: because the LORD made the earth and gives it to whomever he pleases (verse 5), he can give it to Nebuchadnezzar. The final section closes with an unexpected note of hope: the vessels will go to Babylon, but they will come back.

outline.t: The yoke and the message to the envoys
The Creator gives the lands to Nebuchadnezzar
To Zedekiah: serve Babylon and live
To priests and people: the temple vessels will go, and return

doctrines.note: The LORD speaks as the maker of the earth who gives it to whom he pleases (verse 5). Empires rise and fall at his word, and Babylon's power has a time limit (verse 7). This is said not only to Judah but to the kings of other nations.

Submission to Babylon is not presented as defeat but as God's way through the crisis. Life in the land, and later life in exile, lay on the path of accepting what God had appointed, not in heroic resistance.
False prophecy here is not obviously pagan. It uses the LORD's name and promises what everyone wants to hear. The test is whether the message matches what God has actually said.

words.note: Ol, yoke. It is the central image of the chapter and the next. The Bible uses it both for oppressive rule and for rightful service, and the question in these chapters is whose yoke Judah will accept.

Keli, a vessel, article, or utensil, a broad word for any made object. Here it means the sacred furnishings of the temple. Their fate was a test of faith: if they went to Babylon, God's promise to bring them back (verse 22) was all that remained.
Avad, to serve or work, from the same root as the word for servant. The verb runs through the chapter. To serve the king of Babylon, in this setting, is to submit to the LORD's own decision.

christ: The chapter's link to Jesus is thematic rather than predictive. It shows the God of Israel ruling all nations and using even a foreign emperor, which is the backdrop for the New Testament's claim that God sent his Son in the days of Caesar Augustus and that all authority in heaven and earth has now been given to the risen Christ (Matthew 28:18). Jesus also used the yoke image, inviting the weary to take his yoke upon them because it is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:29-30). The contrast is instructive: the yoke of Babylon was a discipline to be endured for a season, while Christ's yoke is the rule of a gentle master. And the promise that the temple vessels would come back after exile belongs to the larger hope of restored worship that the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus, who spoke of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21).

hard.q: Was Jeremiah telling his people to collaborate with a tyrant? Does this mean God always wants submission to oppressive powers?
hard.a: In his own day many saw Jeremiah as a defeatist or even a traitor (37:13-14). But his counsel was not a general political theory. It rested on a specific word from God about a specific empire for a limited time (verse 7; 25:11-12), given to a nation under judgment for its covenant unfaithfulness. Babylon was not righteous; Jeremiah also announced its punishment (chapters 50 to 51). Readers have drawn different lessons from this. Some see a principle that God's people should not place their hope in political revolt or national survival. Others caution against turning a particular prophetic command into a rule for every situation, noting that Scripture also honors resistance to tyranny in other settings (the midwives in Exodus 1, Daniel's friends in Daniel 3). What the chapter clearly teaches is that God, not the empire and not national pride, decides the times, and that faith sometimes means accepting a hard path rather than a heroic one.

questions: The false prophets offered a message of quick deliverance. Why are messages of quick relief so attractive, and how do you test them?
Jeremiah wore a yoke in public to make his point. What might it cost to embody a hard message rather than only speak it?
The temple vessels would go to Babylon and come back. How do you hold onto a promise when the thing you value is being taken away?
